paragraphs.text: Every human body carries a vast population of microbes. Bacteria, fungi and viruses live on the skin, in the mouth and above all in the gut, where their numbers are comparable to the number of human cells in the body. For most of the twentieth century, these organisms attracted attention mainly when they caused disease, and the great achievement of medicine was learning to kill them. Over the past two decades, however, researchers have come to see the community of microbes in the gut, now usually called the microbiome, as something closer to an organ in its own right, one that people depend on as much as it depends on them. Estimates of their number have been revised as methods have improved, but the scale is not in doubt: the total weight of the gut bacteria is roughly that of a small bag of sugar.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Much of this change was made possible by new techniques. Most gut bacteria cannot easily be grown in a laboratory, because they are adapted to the airless conditions inside the intestine, so for a long time scientists had little idea what was there. The ability to read the genetic material in a sample of faeces allowed researchers to identify bacteria without growing them, and revealed that each person carries hundreds of species, in combinations that differ markedly from one individual to another. Around a third of the species found in a typical person are shared with most other people; the rest vary. Samples from people in different countries show especially large differences, reflecting diet and way of life.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The microbes perform tasks that the body cannot perform alone. They break down fibre from plants that human enzymes cannot digest, producing substances that nourish the cells lining the gut and may reduce inflammation. They make certain vitamins, help to train the immune system in early life and occupy space that might otherwise be taken by harmful bacteria. Experiments in mice raised in completely sterile conditions, with no microbes at all, have shown abnormalities in the development of their guts and immune systems, which can be partly corrected by introducing bacteria. Some gut bacteria also influence how the body stores fat and responds to certain medicines.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The composition of the microbiome is shaped from birth. Babies acquire their first microbes from their mothers during birth and from breast milk, and the community changes rapidly during the first few years of life before becoming relatively stable. Babies born by caesarean section have noticeably different early microbiomes, although the differences largely disappear within a year or two. Diet is the most important influence in adulthood: people who eat a wide variety of plant foods tend to have more diverse gut communities than those whose diet is dominated by processed food. Older people tend to have less diverse communities, although the reasons are not yet clear.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Antibiotics are the most powerful disruption. A course of treatment kills harmful bacteria but also large numbers of harmless ones, and although most communities recover within weeks, some species may take months to return or disappear altogether. In a small number of patients, repeated antibiotic use allows a particular harmful bacterium to take over the gut, causing severe illness. In such cases, transferring stool from a healthy donor has proved remarkably effective, curing most patients in trials where antibiotics had failed. The procedure is now offered in some hospitals for this specific infection, under careful screening of donors.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Many other claims about the microbiome are less secure. Differences in gut bacteria have been reported in people with obesity, depression, allergies and many other conditions, but in most cases it is not clear whether the bacteria contribute to the condition or merely reflect it, since illness and its treatment can themselves change the gut. Some striking results have come from mice, whose guts differ considerably from those of humans. Researchers increasingly warn that the field has been overpromised, and that very few treatments based on it have yet been shown to work. Studies that follow people over many years are beginning to separate cause from effect.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: This caution applies to products sold to the public. Probiotic supplements, which contain live bacteria, are widely available, but the bacteria they contain often do not settle in the gut and are simply passed through within days. Some specific products have shown benefits for particular conditions, but general claims that they improve health in people who are already well are mostly unsupported. Research suggests that the overall pattern of diet has a larger influence on the gut community than any supplement. Fermented foods such as yoghurt contain live bacteria too, but their long-term effects are still being studied.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The idea that each of us is an ecosystem rather than a single organism has nonetheless changed the way many biologists think. It has encouraged more careful use of antibiotics, prompted research into how diet influences health through microbes, and raised new questions about how the modern environment, with its processed food and reduced contact with soil and animals, may be affecting communities that evolved alongside humans over millions of years. The garden inside us is only beginning to be mapped. Mapping it fully will take many more years of careful work.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: Rust is so familiar that it seems almost natural, and in a sense it is. Most metals used in construction and industry, including iron, are found in the ground not as pure metals but combined with oxygen as ores, and considerable energy must be spent to separate them. Once refined, they tend to return to their more stable combined form whenever they are exposed to air and water. Corrosion, of which rusting is the most common example, is the gradual reversal of the process by which the metal was made, and it has sometimes been called a slow fire. The name reflects the chemistry: burning and rusting both involve a reaction with oxygen, one fast and one slow.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The cost of this slow reversal is enormous. Studies in several countries have estimated that corrosion costs the equivalent of around three per cent of national economic output each year, through the repair and replacement of bridges, pipelines, ships, cars and machinery, and through the protective measures taken to prevent it. Corrosion has also caused disasters: bridges have collapsed and pipelines burst because steel hidden inside concrete or underground was weakened without anyone noticing. Much of this cost could be avoided, according to the same studies, if existing knowledge were applied more consistently.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Rusting is an electrochemical process, similar in principle to what happens inside a battery. Where water containing dissolved oxygen touches iron, some parts of the surface give up electrons and the iron dissolves, while at other parts oxygen and water take up those electrons. The dissolved iron then combines with oxygen and water to form hydrated iron oxide, the reddish-brown material we call rust. Salt greatly speeds up the process because it makes the water a better conductor, which is why cars rust faster in places where salt is spread on winter roads and why ships and coastal structures suffer so badly. Dry air causes little corrosion, which is why iron objects survive well in deserts.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Unlike the oxide that forms on some other metals, rust does not protect the metal beneath it. It is porous and flaky, and it occupies several times the volume of the iron from which it formed, so it breaks away and exposes fresh metal to further attack. When steel reinforcing bars inside concrete rust, the expansion can crack the surrounding concrete from within, allowing more water in and speeding up the damage. Aluminium, by contrast, forms a thin, tightly attached oxide layer that seals the surface and prevents further corrosion, which is why aluminium objects can last for decades outdoors without protection. Copper roofs turn green for a similar reason, forming a stable surface layer that protects the metal beneath.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The simplest defence is to keep water and oxygen away from the metal with paint or other coatings, which must be maintained, since any scratch allows corrosion to begin. A more ingenious method takes advantage of the electrochemistry of rusting. If iron is connected to a metal that gives up electrons more readily, such as zinc, the zinc corrodes instead, sacrificing itself to protect the iron. Steel coated with zinc, known as galvanised steel, is protected in this way even where the coating is scratched, and blocks of zinc or magnesium are attached to ship hulls and buried pipelines for the same purpose. Some pipelines are protected by a small electric current that achieves the same effect.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Another approach is to change the metal itself. Stainless steel, developed in the early twentieth century, contains chromium, which forms a thin, invisible oxide layer similar to that on aluminium and repairs itself if scratched. Stainless steel is widely used for kitchen equipment, medical instruments and buildings, but it is considerably more expensive than ordinary steel. Some structural steels contain small amounts of copper and other elements that allow them to form a stable, dark layer of rust that protects the metal beneath, and such weathering steel is used for bridges and sculptures that are left unpainted. Weathering steel needs careful design, since water that collects in joints can prevent the protective layer from forming.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Engineers increasingly rely on monitoring rather than simply on protection. Sensors embedded in concrete can detect the conditions that allow reinforcing steel to corrode, and drones and robots can inspect bridges and pipelines that are difficult to reach. Some newer structures use reinforcing bars made of materials that do not rust at all, such as fibre-reinforced plastics, although these behave differently under load and are not suitable for every purpose. Records from inspections are increasingly analysed by computer to predict where corrosion is likely next.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Corrosion can never be eliminated, since the chemistry that drives it is the same chemistry that makes metals useful in the first place. What engineers can do is slow it, direct it and detect it before it causes harm. The choice between different methods is usually a matter of cost: a coating that must be renewed every decade may be cheaper in the short term but more expensive over the life of a structure than a more durable solution chosen at the start. Engineers therefore increasingly consider the whole life of a structure when choosing materials.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Can we pull carbon out of the air?

paragraphs.text: Most efforts to limit climate change concentrate on reducing the amount of carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere. In recent years, however, attention has also turned to removing carbon dioxide that is already there. Several approaches have been proposed, from planting forests to spreading crushed rock on fields, but the one that has attracted the most investment and the most controversy is direct air capture: machines that draw in ordinary air, extract the carbon dioxide from it and store it permanently underground. Removal is not a new idea, but only recently has it attracted serious money, and its supporters and critics often talk past each other.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The chemistry is well understood. Air is passed over materials that bind carbon dioxide, which are then heated or otherwise treated to release it as a concentrated gas that can be compressed and injected into suitable rock formations. Sophie Brandt, a chemical engineer, explains that the fundamental difficulty is dilution. Carbon dioxide makes up only about 0.04 per cent of the air, so enormous volumes must be processed to capture a meaningful quantity, and separating it requires considerable energy, most of it as heat. Some plants use liquids rather than solids to capture the gas, but the principle is similar. Storage sites must be chosen carefully so that the gas cannot leak back to the surface.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Kwame Asante, a climate scientist, argues that some form of carbon removal will be necessary whatever else is done. Certain activities, such as aviation, some heavy industry and parts of agriculture, will be extremely difficult to make free of emissions within the next few decades, and removing an equivalent amount of carbon dioxide may be the only way to balance them. Most scenarios that limit warming to the levels agreed internationally, he notes, assume that large quantities of carbon will be removed from the atmosphere later this century. He adds that natural methods, such as restoring forests and soils, have limits of their own, since land is needed for food and the carbon stored may be released by fire or drought.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The question is how much of that removal direct air capture can provide, and at what cost. Current plants capture relatively small amounts, measured in thousands of tonnes a year, while the scale imagined in climate scenarios runs to billions. Lucia Moreno, an energy economist, points out that capturing a tonne of carbon dioxide from the air currently costs several times as much as preventing a tonne from being emitted in most other ways, such as replacing coal-fired power with renewable energy. She argues that until costs fall dramatically, money spent on direct air capture would achieve more if spent on cutting emissions. Estimates of future costs vary widely, and many depend on assumptions about technologies that have not yet been built. Some of the largest planned plants aim to capture a million tonnes a year.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Supporters reply that costs have fallen in other clean technologies, such as solar panels and batteries, once they were produced at scale, and that early investment is necessary to bring about similar reductions. Brandt accepts the comparison in part, but cautions that direct air capture faces a physical limit that solar panels did not: the energy needed to separate a dilute gas cannot be reduced below a certain minimum, however good the engineering becomes. Supporters also point out that capture plants can be built in modules, which may help costs fall with repetition. The history of other technologies offers examples of both outcomes.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: A different concern is political rather than technical. Erik Nystrom, who studies environmental policy, warns that the promise of future removal may be used to justify continued emissions today, allowing companies and governments to delay difficult changes on the assumption that the carbon can be taken back later. He points out that some of the largest investors in direct air capture are oil companies, and argues that removal should be treated as an addition to emission cuts, never a substitute for them. Some companies have already sold removal credits to other firms wishing to offset their emissions.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The energy the machines require raises a further issue. If a plant is powered by electricity from fossil fuels, it may release much of the carbon it captures, and even when renewable power is used, that power could otherwise have replaced fossil fuels elsewhere. Asante therefore argues that direct air capture makes most sense in places with abundant clean energy that cannot easily be used for other purposes, such as remote regions with strong geothermal or solar resources, and suitable rock for storing the gas. Several of the first large plants have been built in regions that meet these conditions.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Direct air capture is neither a solution to climate change nor an illusion. It is an expensive and energy-hungry technology that may eventually play a useful part in balancing emissions that cannot be avoided, provided it develops alongside, rather than instead of, the rapid reduction of emissions. Deciding how much public money it deserves, and under what conditions, is a question that will become more pressing as the plants grow larger. Its future will also depend on how carefully the storage of carbon is monitored over centuries.
paragraphs.label: H

explanation.ru: «Current plants capture relatively small amounts, measured in thousands of tonnes a year, while the scale imagined in climate scenarios runs to billions» → NO. Тысячи тонн против миллиардов — текст противоречит; это NO, а не NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: Several of the first large plants have been built in regions that meet these conditions
items.prompt: Most direct air capture plants are located in remote regions.

explanation.en: “Several of the first” is not “most”; no proportion is given → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: «Several of the first» — алғашқы бірнешеуі, көпшілігі емес; үлесі айтылмаған → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: «Several of the first» — несколько первых, а не большинство; доля не указана → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: costs have fallen in other clean technologies, such as solar panels and batteries
items.prompt: The cost of direct air capture has fallen faster than that of solar panels.

explanation.en: Solar panel costs have fallen, but no comparison of speed is made → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Күн панельдерінің арзандағаны айтылған, бірақ ұстау технологиясымен салыстыру жоқ → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Упомянуто падение цен на солнечные панели, но сравнения скорости с улавливанием нет → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: provided it develops alongside, rather than instead of, the rapid reduction of emissions
items.prompt: Direct air capture should replace efforts to cut emissions.

explanation.en: “provided it develops alongside, rather than instead of, the rapid reduction of emissions” → NO. “alongside, rather than instead of” rejects replacement — NO.
explanation.kk: «provided it develops alongside, rather than instead of, the rapid reduction of emissions» → NO. «alongside, rather than instead of» — автор алмастыруға қарсы; бұл NO.
explanation.ru: «provided it develops alongside, rather than instead of, the rapid reduction of emissions» → NO. «alongside, rather than instead of» — автор против замены; это NO.
